Action Plan:
1. Arrange in-person clinic appointment for full physical examination focusing on cardiovascular and respiratory systems.  
2. Order blood tests including thyroid function (to assess current thyroxine status) at time of visit.  
3. Evaluate severe intermittent frontal headaches during the visit; include neurological examination.  
4. Review episodes of bilateral arm tingling, palpitations, and episodic shortness of breath at the appointment.  
5. Assess recent 5-lb unintentional weight loss, reduced appetite, heat intolerance, and loss of libido; correlate findings with thyroid panel and stress levels.  
6. Advise patient to book appointment via practice app; clinician will brief colleague in advance to avoid duplication of history taking.  
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• 35-year-old male lawyer presents with feeling hot and severe frontal headaches that occur at work while on computer or in meetings; started after changing jobs.  
• Associated symptoms (mostly episodic, one at a time):  
  – Palpitations (~ once/day, sometimes in elevator or at desk).  
  – Shortness of breath while seated at desk; none with exercise.  
  – Tingling (“quick pricking”) in both arms; no leg involvement.  
  – Reduced appetite with unintentional 5-lb weight loss; clothes not noticeably looser; no external comments.  
  – Loss of libido since job change.  
• Stress at work rated 7–8/10.  
• No previous history of similar headaches.  
Past Medical History: Hyperthyroidism (patient label); currently on thyroxine.  
Medications: Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Social History: Works as lawyer in London; alcohol once/week (couple of glasses of wine); non-smoker; denies recreational drug use.  
Allergies: None reported.

Objective:
• Telehealth visit – no vitals or physical examination performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Multisystem symptoms (heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, libido loss):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism due to excessive thyroxine replacement (DDx: High).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Endogenous hyperthyroidism (Graves disease / toxic multinodular goitre – Low-Medium).  
     • Stress-related/anxiety disorder (Medium).  
   - Investigations planned: Thyroid function tests (TFTs) at upcoming visit.  
   - Treatment planned: Adjust thyroxine dose if TFTs confirm biochemical hyperthyroidism (to be determined post-results).  

2. Severe intermittent frontal headaches:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Stress-related tension or migraine-type headache (DDx: Medium).  
   - Differential diagnosis: Intracranial mass lesion (Low); anxiety-related muscle tension; hypertension (no BP yet).  
   - Investigations planned: Neurological and blood pressure examination at in-person visit; further imaging only if red-flag signs emerge.  
   - Treatment planned: To be decided after examination; consider ergonomic advice, simple analgesia, stress management strategies.

3. Episodic bilateral arm tingling & shortness of breath:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Hyperventilation/anxiety episodes (part of stress response).  
   - Differential diagnosis: Paroxysmal arrhythmia (e.g., SVT); vitamin B12 deficiency; thyroid excess–related paresthesia.  
   - Investigations planned: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination during visit; TFTs (as above).  
   - Treatment planned: Guided by examination findings and lab results; consider stress reduction techniques.

4. Loss of libido:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Likely secondary to hyperthyroid state or chronic work stress.  
   - Differential diagnosis: Depression, other endocrine causes (e.g., low testosterone) – to explore if persists after thyroid/stress management.  
   - Investigations planned: Monitor after TFT results; additional endocrine tests if clinically indicated.  
   - Treatment planned: Address underlying cause once identified.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Vitals, detailed medication dose, complete review of systems, family history.  
● No internal conflicts identified between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor pauses/fillers but clinically adequate.
